lesson.title: Sliding Window: Keeping the Pipe Full While Staying Reliable
lesson.summary: The sliding window protocol generalizes ARQ by letting a sender have multiple frames in flight simultaneously, using a window of permitted sequence numbers that advances as acknowledgments arrive, which lets a link's throughput approach its actual bandwidth instead of being capped by round trip delay.
lesson.body:
Stop and wait's central flaw is that it wastes the round trip time: the sender transmits one frame's worth of data and then goes idle for an entire RTT waiting on its acknowledgment. The sliding window protocol fixes this by allowing the sender to have up to N unacknowledged frames outstanding at once, where N is the window size. As long as the window is not full, the sender keeps transmitting new frames back to back without waiting for each individual acknowledgment first. This is the key idea that lets the sender's effective throughput approach the link's raw bandwidth rather than being capped by the inverse of the round trip time.

The window is best pictured as a range of sequence numbers that slides forward over time. At any instant the sender has a set of sequence numbers it is allowed to use: the lowest is the oldest frame sent but not yet acknowledged, and the highest is that lowest value plus N minus one. When an acknowledgment arrives confirming a frame has been received, the window slides forward, freeing up a new sequence number at the top that the sender can now use for a new frame. The receiver maintains its own window over sequence numbers it is willing to accept, and the size of that receive window is what determines how go back N and selective repeat diverge from each other later in this unit.

A worked example makes the mechanics concrete. Suppose the sender's window size is 4 and sequence numbers run 0 through 7, a 3 bit field wrapping after 7 back to 0. Initially the sender's window covers sequence numbers 0, 1, 2, and 3. It sends frames 0, 1, 2, and 3 without waiting for individual acknowledgments. An acknowledgment for frame 0 arrives, so the window slides to cover 1, 2, 3, and 4, and the sender is now free to transmit frame 4. Shortly after, an acknowledgment for frame 1 arrives, sliding the window to 2, 3, 4, and 5, and frame 5 can go out. If the window ever fills completely, all N sequence numbers used and unacknowledged, the sender must stop and wait, exactly as in the earlier protocol, until the oldest outstanding frame is acknowledged and the window can slide again.

Choosing the window size N is a direct application of the bandwidth delay product that shaped ARQ's throughput concerns. To keep the pipe continuously full, N should be large enough that the sender never runs out of new sequence numbers before the first acknowledgment of the current batch comes back, roughly N equal to bandwidth multiplied by RTT, divided by the frame size. Too small a window reintroduces stop and wait style idle time. Too large a window relative to the sequence number space risks ambiguity between old and new frames after wraparound, which is why the sequence number field must be sized with the window size in mind.

Sliding window by itself only describes how many frames may be outstanding. It does not yet specify what the receiver does when a frame arrives out of order or gets lost partway through a batch. Those choices are exactly what distinguish go back N, which discards anything out of order and forces the sender to resend a whole run of frames, from selective repeat, which buffers out of order frames and asks only for the specific missing one to be resent.
